```{.quiz-yaml}
id: 15_related_anova_columns_and_rows
title: Columns and rows
questions:
  - id: within_a_column
    type: multiple-select
    prompt: >
      Chapter 14's ANOVA would treat each column of the table as a group. Start
      with the variability *within* a group. Look down the first column, at the
      five children's times on their first race alone. Which of these could
      help explain why those five times differ from one another?
    options:
      - text: Some kids are just faster than others overall
        correct: true
      - text: Practice or competition
      - text: Chance, like a particularly good or bad run
        correct: true
    explanation: >
      Everyone in a group ran the same race, so practice and competition can't
      be the reason, just as in Chapter 14. But these are five different kids,
      each of whom could have a good or bad run.

  - id: between_column_averages
    type: multiple-select
    prompt: >
      Now the differences *between* the groups. The three column means are in
      the $M$ row of the table: 50.20, 47.40, and 42.40 seconds. Which of
      these could help explain why those three means differ from one another?
    options:
      - text: Some kids are just faster than others overall
      - text: Practice or competition
        correct: true
      - text: Chance, like a particularly good or bad run
        correct: true
    hint: >
      Clyde's times count toward all three means. Could he make one of them
      lower than the others?
    explanation: >
      The same five children are in every group. Clyde pulls all three means
      down by about the same amount, so the kids' overall speed can't make one
      group's mean differ from another's. It's part of the variability within
      groups, but not of the differences between them.

  - id: between_row_averages
    type: multiple-select
    prompt: >
      Now group the scores across the table instead, taking each child's three
      times as a group. Each of those groups has a mean too: about 34 seconds
      for Clyde, and about 52 for Mary. Which of these could help explain why
      the children's means differ from one another?
    options:
      - text: Some kids are just faster than others overall
        correct: true
      - text: Practice or competition
      - text: Chance, like a particularly good or bad run
        correct: true
    hint: >
      Which races go into Clyde's mean? Which go into Mary's?
    explanation: >
      Every child's mean is made up of the same three races, so practice and
      competition affect them all alike. The children's means differ because
      of their overall speed, plus a bit of chance.

  - id: no_chance_pattern
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Last one. Imagine there were no chance at all: each child has their own
      overall speed, and each race speeds everyone up or slows everyone down by
      the same amount. What would we see in the table?
    options:
      - text: Every child would have the same three times as every other child
      - text: Each child's three times would be identical
      - text: Every child's times would change by the same amount from one race to the next
        correct: true
    explanation: >
      The children would still sit at different levels, and the races would
      still differ, but every child's times would follow the same pattern. The
      real ones don't: Stephen sped up by 1 second and then by 7, Bertha by 7
      and then by 1. So there's some variability that neither the kids'
      overall speed nor the races account for.
```
